lesson.title: Activation Energy: The Barrier Every Reaction Must Climb First
lesson.summary: Activation energy is the energy input required to get reactants over an energy barrier and into a reactive state, a hurdle that exists regardless of whether the overall reaction releases or absorbs energy, and one that enzymes dramatically lower.
lesson.body:
Activation energy, often abbreviated Ea, is the minimum amount of energy that reactant molecules must absorb before they can be converted into products. It is easy to assume that an exergonic reaction, one with an overall negative delta G, should happen instantly and spontaneously, but this confuses the overall energy change of a reaction with the size of the barrier standing between reactants and products. Even a reaction that releases a great deal of energy overall may require a substantial initial push before it can proceed, in the same way a boulder resting in a small dip at the top of a hill needs a nudge over the lip before it will roll downhill on its own, even though rolling down clearly releases far more energy than the nudge cost.

This barrier exists because converting reactants into products almost always requires temporarily breaking or weakening existing bonds before new, more stable bonds can form. That in between moment, when old bonds are partly broken and new ones are only partly formed, is a high energy, unstable arrangement, and reaching it costs energy up front even if the final products end up at much lower energy than the starting materials. Activation energy is essentially a measure of how difficult it is to reach that unstable peak, and it is what determines how fast a reaction proceeds at a given temperature, entirely independent of whether the reaction is endergonic or exergonic overall.

Because so many biologically necessary reactions have activation energies too high to be crossed at reasonable rates at normal body temperature, uncatalyzed metabolism would be far too slow to sustain life. This is precisely the problem enzymes solve. An enzyme lowers the activation energy of the specific reaction it catalyzes, allowing a much larger fraction of substrate molecules to react in a given period of time, often speeding up the reaction by factors of a million or more compared to the uncatalyzed process. Crucially, an enzyme accomplishes this without changing the overall free energy difference between reactants and products, meaning it does not make an endergonic reaction favorable, it only makes an already possible reaction go fast enough to matter.

Enzymes lower activation energy through the mechanisms already introduced with the active site and the enzyme substrate complex: binding energy from the enzyme active site can be used to strain particular bonds in the substrate, hold reactive groups in precise alignment, exclude water that might otherwise interfere, and provide catalytic side chains that stabilize the unstable intermediate arrangement the reaction has to pass through. Catalase again offers a good illustration: the uncatalyzed decomposition of hydrogen peroxide has a substantial activation energy barrier and proceeds sluggishly at room temperature, but catalase's active site lowers that barrier so effectively that the same decomposition becomes one of the fastest known enzymatic reactions.

Activation energy connects directly back to the Gibbs free energy framework used to classify reactions as endergonic or exergonic, but it answers a different question. Delta G tells you whether a reaction is thermodynamically favorable and in which direction it will eventually go. Activation energy tells you how fast it will actually get there. Both quantities matter for understanding real biochemistry, and the next concept, the transition state, describes precisely what that unstable, high energy peak at the top of the activation energy barrier looks like.
